newsitem.title: GERMANY: BONN HAS REASON TO BE TOUGH ON EMU - ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: BONN HAS REASON TO BE TOUGH ON EMU - ANALYSTS.

text.p: Germany has compelling domestic political reasons for taking its tough stance on fiscal discipline after European monetary union (EMU) starts in 1999, but it may compromise yet, analysts said on Tuesday.
The German public is nervous of giving up its rock-solid mark for the uncertainties of the Euro, and Chancellor Helmut Kohl is anxious to avoid this becoming an divisive issue in the 1998 election.

Analysts said the hard line finance state secretary Juergen Stark laid down to European finance ministers on Monday was not just a negotiating tactic to toughen up an eventual compromise. It is simply what the German public wants.

Stark said Germany wanted stiff penalties for countries that fail to keep fiscal discipline after the start of EMU, and it wanted to define precisely the circumstances in which they could avoid such penalties.

Germany devised the idea of the stability pact to ensure that meeting the targets sets in the Maastricht treaty on European monetary union is not a one-off event at the start of the future single currency.
Germany's tough stance is "partly tactical and partly serious," said Gerhard Grebe at Bank Julius Baer. Kohl "wants to keep EMU from becoming an election issue in 1998," he said.

Several countries, including Germany, may fail to meet the criteria for inclusion in EMU. This would be an embarrassment for the German government, which has been calling for strict interpretation of the entry criteria, Grebe added.
With its stance, Bonn was preparing the way to say it is safe to be laxer about the entry criteria if the stability pact had the bite to ensure fiscal responsibility after EMU starts.
"It can't be a paper tiger," Grebe said.
But economist Thomas Mayer at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt said he thought the issue was so serious that Germany would not compromise on the essentials of its position.
"The position that Stark has been taking is a highly political position, designed to make sure the government will not open up an unguarded spot and allow the opposition to derail EMU," Mayer said.

Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and other ministers at the Brussels meeting said Germany would not be able to adhere to such a tough stance, as it had only the support of the Netherlands.

Many financial market participants also believe Kohl will soften the German position when the time is right. As with German unification, the chancellor is putting priority on the political opportunity, and will try to grit his teeth and ride out the economic difficulties, they say.

"(Germany is) trying to put as much pressure as possible on its partners to get their deficits down, and to mollify the German public as well," said economist Mathias Haffner at BZW in Frankfurt. "But it seems to be more of a negotiating tactic than something they actually want to achieve."
Some softening of the criteria was inevitable to allow enough countries to participate to make the project meaningful at the start, Haffner said.
If one-off efforts are needed to get deficits into line in 1997 -- when the initial EMU participants are decided -- many countries could find their deficits bulging again in 1998.
This could lead to embarrassing fines in the first year of EMU if Germany keeps its hard line, Haffner said.
But Mayer insisted Germany means business. And the Netherlands may be a small ally, but it will have the EU presidency for the first half of 1997, he said.
"(Stark's) rule-based approach is absolutely essential in this context," Mayer said. "History has shown it is nearly impossible to exercise fiscal discipline where discretion is involved."

Germany will not therefore compromise on its call for a specific definition of "severe recession" -- defined as one in which the economy slumped by two percent in one year, or contracted for four consecutive quarters -- he predicted.
